vignette:
Luca, a fifty-six-year-old guitarist who had played in small clubs and recording studios for nearly four decades, could no longer sit through a rehearsal without his hands trembling. Professionally, he had always prided himself on his steady, lyrical phrasing, but in the months since the assault, his playing had become erratic, punctuated by sudden stops whenever a bandmate shifted too quickly in his peripheral vision. The event itself remained fractured in his mind, like shards of glass he could only glance at before turning away. He knew it had happened backstage after a benefit show, when the tour manager—a tall man whose expensive cologne always lingered in the green room—had cornered him near the equipment cases. What came next was a blur of pain and the metallic scent of his own blood from a split lip, but the details that surfaced most vividly were those he wished he could forget: the manager’s watch scraping against his throat, the way the man’s breath smelled of whiskey, and the perfume—that same sharp, woody cologne—pressed into his face while the manager forced him to his knees. Luca had tried to push back, but the memory always stopped short before he could reach the end. His mind seemed to slam a door just as the worst part began—the feel of the manager’s hand unbuckling his belt, the fabric of his own jeans being pulled down, the degrading weight of the man’s body against his back—leaving him with a few hyper-clear images and a vast blankness where the rest of the story should have been. He could not tell himself, let alone anyone else, what had actually happened in those minutes. Sometimes he would sit in his home studio—the only room where he felt any semblance of safety—and try to force himself through the sequence, but his thoughts would skid sideways and the memory would evaporate before it could take shape.

In the aftermath, Luca had made a rigid set of rules that he never explicitly named but that governed every hour of his days. He stopped returning calls from the musicians he used to drink with after gigs, certain that if he saw them they would bring up the tour manager or ask about why he had quit the band so abruptly. He no longer attended rehearsals in public venues, preferring to practice alone in the cramped room at home that smelled of old wood and cable ties. When his wife, Elena, suggested they go out for dinner, he would find a reason to decline—the restaurant might be crowded, someone might bump into him from behind, or a stranger at the next table might wear a scent that carried even faintly of cedar and musk. That particular cologne had become a landmine. He would detect it on a passerby and immediately feel his chest tighten, his vision narrowing to a single point as he scanned for the nearest exit. The only place he trusted was the small café two blocks from his house, because he knew every angle of the room and could sit with his back to the wall, watching the door.

Anger was a feeling Luca had sworn off entirely. He told himself that losing his temper would only prove that he had been broken by what happened, so he clenched his jaw and smiled through every irritation. But the suppression had a cost: once every few weeks, a trivial annoyance—a dropped cable, a delay in the subway—would ignite something he could not contain, and he would shout or slam a table. The outbursts terrified him, because they felt like a stranger had taken over his body, and afterward he would retreat further into silence. He had also developed a quiet dread of anyone in a uniform or a position of authority. A security guard at a venue, a police officer directing traffic—each made his shoulders hike up and his mind race. He could not explain why, except that the tour manager had worn a dark blazer with a gold badge on the lapel, and now anything resembling that insignia triggered a wave of hypervigilance. Elena had noticed the changes: he no longer wanted to drive past the concert hall where the assault had occurred, he flinched when she touched his shoulder unexpectedly, and he had started locking the bedroom door at night even though they had never locked it before. She had urged him to see someone, but for months he had resisted, insisting that if he just held the memory at bay long enough, it would eventually dissolve.

There was another trigger that Luca had not told anyone about, because it seemed too broad to name. He could not tolerate violence of any kind—not even the staged fights on television. One evening, while flipping channels, he landed on an action movie where two men struggled in a close-quarters brawl, one pinning the other’s shoulders to the floor. Luca’s stomach lurched; the sound of a grunt and the sight of a fist connecting with a jaw sent him reeling. He dropped the remote and sat rigid, his heart hammering, the image in his mind suddenly overlaid with the memory of the tour manager’s watch scraping across his throat, and then the sickening weight of being pinned facedown on the dusty floor. He had to leave the room and stand in the dark backyard, gasping, until the feeling passed. After that, he avoided any film or news segment that showed a physical confrontation, and he also deleted any podcast or radio show that mentioned sexual misconduct or assault, because the words themselves—even spoken by a stranger about a different person—made his throat close up and his vision blur. He would change the channel abruptly or leave the room when a heated argument on a talk show seemed about to escalate. Even a YouTube clip of a fan shaking a musician on stage—something he would have once dismissed as part of the scene—now made him feel as though he were back in that equipment case, unable to move, the manager’s breath hot on his neck.

And then there was blood. Luca had always been casual about minor cuts—a guitar string snapping and nicking his finger was part of the trade. But after the assault, the sight of blood, even a single drop, became unbearable. One afternoon, changing a string, he pricked his thumb on a fresh wire and a small bead of red welled up. He stared at it, frozen, and suddenly the metallic scent from that night flooded his nostrils—the taste of his own split lip, the smear of it across his cheek when the manager’s watch caught his mouth. Luca dropped the guitar, grabbed a towel, and scrubbed at his thumb until the bleeding stopped, then stood in the bathroom with his eyes closed, waiting for his heart to slow. Since then, he had become compulsively careful with any sharp object, and he avoided watching medical scenes on television or even looking at a paper cut on Elena’s hand. The color red in a certain shade, especially dark crimson, would make him veer his gaze away. He had not cut himself since the first incident; he simply could not bear to see his own blood again, because it took him straight back to the floor of that backstage room, the taste of copper on his tongue, the manager’s weight pressing him down. What finally brought him to the clinic was a morning in early spring when he caught a whiff of that cologne—or thought he did—while waiting for the train. In a flash of disorientation, he turned and nearly struck an elderly man who had tapped his arm to ask for the time. The man was apologetic; Luca had been the one to spin around with his fist raised. He spent the rest of the day locked in his studio, shaking, and that evening he told Elena he would accept her offer to find a therapist. As he sat across from the clinician, he could feel the edge of the memory pressing against the door in his mind—the pressure of the manager’s hands, the humiliation of being forced to submit—and he was terrified that if he let it in fully, he would lose whatever fragile sense of control he had left. But he also knew that the life he was living—hemmed in by safe zones, emptied of friends, haunted by smells, shadows, blood, the mere sight of a clenched fist, and the sound of a belt buckle unclasping in a movie—was no longer a life he could sustain. He needed someone to help him see the whole story, even if the seeing broke him first.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a morning in early spring when he caught a whiff of that cologne—or thought he did—while waiting for the train. In a flash of disorientation, he turned and nearly struck an elderly man who had tapped his arm to ask for the time. The man was apologetic; Luca had been the one to spin around with his fist raised. He spent the rest of the day locked in his studio, shaking, and that evening he told Elena he would accept her offer to find a therapist. As he sat across from the clinician, he could feel the edge of the memory pressing against the door in his mind—the pressure of the manager’s hands, the humiliation of being forced to submit—and he was terrified that if he let it in fully, he would lose whatever fragile sense of control he had left. But he also knew that the life he was living—hemmed in by safe zones, emptied of friends, haunted by smells, shadows, blood, the mere sight of a clenched fist, and the sound of a belt buckle unclasping in a movie—was no longer a life he could sustain. He needed someone to help him see the whole story, even if the seeing broke him first.
